items.title: Gaussian, gamma and beta product integrals
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
For $a>0$ and an integer $r\ge0$, define $I_r(a):=\int_{\mathbb R}x^{2r}e^{-ax^2}\,dx$ as the two-sided improper Riemann integral. Then

$$I_r(a)=\frac{\Gamma(r+\tfrac12)}{a^{r+1/2}},\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}x^{2r+1}e^{-ax^2}\,dx=0,$$

where $\Gamma(s):=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$ for $s>0$. In particular, $I_0(a)=\sqrt{\pi/a}$ and $I_1(a)=\sqrt\pi/(2a^{3/2})$. For every compact interval $K=[a_0,a_1]\subset(0,\infty)$, $I_r$ is continuously differentiable on $K$ and

$$I_r'(a)=-I_{r+1}(a).$$

For $s,t>0$, put $B(s,t):=\int_0^1u^{s-1}(1-u)^{t-1}\,du$. Then $B(s,t)$ is finite and

$$\Gamma(s)\Gamma(t)=\Gamma(s+t)B(s,t),\qquad \Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s),\qquad \Gamma(\tfrac12)=\sqrt\pi.$$

Consequently, if independent positive random variables have densities $x^{s-1}e^{-x}/\Gamma(s)$ and $x^{t-1}e^{-x}/\Gamma(t)$, their sum has density $x^{s+t-1}e^{-x}/\Gamma(s+t)$.
items.strategy:
1.1 For $s>0$, the gamma integrand on $(0,1)$ is bounded by $t^{s-1}$, whose integral is $1/s$. For $t\ge1$, $t^{s-1}e^{-t/2}$ is bounded, so $t^{s-1}e^{-t}\le C_se^{-t/2}$ and the tail converges. On a compact positive $s$-interval, the lower endpoint bounds the near-zero power and the upper endpoint bounds the exponential tail uniformly. Hence $\Gamma(s)$ is finite and has controlled endpoint tails. [given, algebra]

1.2 Let $I=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-x^2}dx$. By [F2], $I^2$ equals the nonnegative plane Gaussian integral, and [F3] evaluates that integral as $\pi$. Hence $I^2=\pi$. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], $I$ is finite and positive. The positive square root in step 1.2 is therefore $I=\sqrt\pi$. [F1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Integration by parts on $[\varepsilon,R]$ gives $\int_\varepsilon^R t^se^{-t}\,dt=[-t^se^{-t}]_\varepsilon^R+s\int_\varepsilon^R t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$. The boundary terms vanish by step 1.1, so $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$; direct integration gives $\Gamma(1)=1$. [step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 For $s,t>0$, the beta integrand is integrable near $0$ by comparison with $u^{s-1}$ and near $1$ by comparison with $(1-u)^{t-1}$. On each compact rectangle $[1/j,j]^2$ the continuous product integrand $x^{s-1}y^{t-1}e^{-(x+y)}$ has integral equal to the product of its one-dimensional integrals, as follows by factoring the finite rectangular Riemann sums. These nested rectangles exhaust the positive quadrant and their integrals tend to $\Gamma(s)\Gamma(t)$ by step 1.1. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Substitution $t=x^2$ on compact half-intervals and passage to the convergent improper limits gives $\Gamma(\tfrac12)=2\int_0^\infty e^{-x^2}\,dx=I=\sqrt\pi$ by steps 1.2 and 2.1. [step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 On $A_j=[1/j,j]\times[1/j,1-1/j]$ in coordinates $(r,u)$, the map $\Phi(r,u)=(ru,r(1-u))$ is injective, has determinant $-r\ne0$, and is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism on an open neighborhood. Its image is a compact Jordan set. The images exhaust the positive quadrant cofinally with the rectangles in step 2.3: each compact rectangle stays a positive distance from both axes and has bounded $x+y$, while each image is compact and stays away from the axes. Applying [F4] on $A_j$ and taking the increasing limits gives $\Gamma(s)\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty r^{s+t-1}e^{-r}\,dr\,B(s,t)=\Gamma(s+t)B(s,t)$. The limits are finite by step 1.1 and the endpoint bounds in step 2.3. [step 1.1, step 2.3, F4, algebra]

4.1 For integer $r\ge0$, $x^{2r}e^{-ax^2/2}$ is bounded on $\mathbb R$, so $x^{2r}e^{-ax^2}\le C e^{-ax^2/2}$ and [F1] gives absolute convergence; odd moments converge absolutely and vanish by reflection. On compact intervals the substitution $y=\sqrt a\,x$ is covered by [F4], and its improper limit gives $I_0(a)=a^{-1/2}I_0(1)=\sqrt{\pi/a}$ by steps 1.2 and 2.1. The substitution $t=ax^2$ on both half-lines gives $I_r(a)=a^{-r-1/2}\Gamma(r+\tfrac12)$; finiteness follows from step 1.1, the half-integer starting value from step 3.1, and recurrence from step 2.2. [given, F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Fix the integer $r\ge0$. Step 4.1 evaluated $I_r(a)=\Gamma(r+\tfrac12)a^{-r-1/2}$ for every $a>0$ using only convergent improper substitutions, and step 2.2 proved the Gamma recurrence by integration by parts; neither argument used parameter differentiation. By [F5], differentiation of this established explicit function gives $$I_r'(a)=-(r+\tfrac12)\Gamma(r+\tfrac12)a^{-r-3/2}=-\Gamma(r+\tfrac32)a^{-r-3/2}=-I_{r+1}(a).$$ The same positive-base power formula makes this derivative continuous on $(0,\infty)$, hence on a neighborhood of every compact $K\subset(0,\infty)$. This proves the full parameter clause without interchanging a derivative and an improper integral. [F5, step 2.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Let $C=[c,d]\subset(0,\infty)$ and set $Q_j=[1/j,j]^2$. The event $A_j=Q_j\cap\{(x,y):x+y\in C\}$ is Jordan measurable. On each grid rectangle $I\times J\subset Q_j$, independence gives probability $P(X\in I)P(Y\in J)=(\int_I f_s)(\int_J f_t)$; because the marginal densities are continuous on $Q_j$, the finite rectangular Riemann sums factor and converge to the integral of $f_s(x)f_t(y)$ on that rectangle. The inner and outer grid unions for $A_j$ differ only in cells meeting its finitely many line-segment boundary pieces; their total area tends to zero, and $f_sf_t$ is bounded on $Q_j$. Thus $P((X,Y)\in A_j)=\int_{A_j}f_sf_t\,dx\,dy$. As $Q_j$ increases to the positive quadrant, countable additivity gives probabilities increasing to $P(X+Y\in C)$, and the nonnegative improper integrals increase to the integral over $x,y>0$. The images of $C\times[1/j,1-1/j]$ under $(r,u)\mapsto(ru,r(1-u))$ increase to $A_C=\{x,y>0:x+y\in C\}$. On each such compact set the map is injective with absolute Jacobian $r$, so [F4] transforms the integral to $r^{s+t-1}e^{-r}u^{s-1}(1-u)^{t-1}/(\Gamma(s)\Gamma(t))$. Its rectangular Riemann sums factor; as $j\to\infty$ the $u$-integral tends to $B(s,t)$. By step 3.2, $P(X+Y\in C)=\int_C r^{s+t-1}e^{-r}/\Gamma(s+t)\,dr$. A singleton C has probability zero by the same zero-area grid-boundary argument. The density integrates to one by step 1.1, so these interval probabilities determine the sum law. [given, step 1.1, step 3.2, F4, algebra] ∎

items.title: Jacobian identity for a specified smooth diffeomorphic flow
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. Suppose $\chi:I\times U\to\mathbb R^n$ is jointly $C^2$, each $\chi_t(a):=\chi(t,a)$ is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism from $U$ onto an open set $U_t$, and $\chi_0(a)=a$. Let $D:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in U_t\}$ be open and let $b:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ with $\partial_t\chi(t,a)=b(t,\chi(t,a))$. Define $F(t,a):=D_a\chi(t,a)$, $J(t,a):=\det F(t,a)$, and $\operatorname{div}b:=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_{x_i}b_i$. Then

$$\partial_tF=(D_xb)(t,\chi)F,\qquad \partial_tJ=J(\operatorname{div}b)(t,\chi),\qquad J(0,a)=1.$$

In particular $J(t,a)>0$ for all $(t,a)\in I\times U$, and if $\operatorname{div}b=0$ on $D$, then $J(t,a)=1$. The same identities hold on the flat torus $\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\Lambda$, where $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\ell_1+\cdots+\mathbb Z\ell_n$ for a linearly independent basis $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n$ and the smooth structure and Euclidean metric descend from $\mathbb R^n$. In that clause, let $\chi:I\times\mathbb T^n\to\mathbb T^n$ be jointly $C^2$, with each $\chi_t$ a diffeomorphism and $\chi_0=\operatorname{id}$. Let $\pi:T\mathbb T^n\to\mathbb T^n$ be the tangent-bundle projection, and let $b:I\times\mathbb T^n\to T\mathbb T^n$ have $C^1$ chart coefficients and satisfy $\pi(b(t,a))=a$ and $\partial_t\chi(t,a)=b(t,\chi(t,a))$. In every translation chart write $b=\sum_i b^i\partial_{x^i}$ and define $\operatorname{div}b:=\sum_i\partial_{x^i}b^i$. Define $F(t,a)$ to be the matrix of $D_a\chi_t:T_a\mathbb T^n\to T_{\chi_t(a)}\mathbb T^n$ in the translation frames and $J(t,a):=\det F(t,a)$. Translation-chart changes have derivative $I$, so these matrices, determinants and divergences agree on overlaps. These are identities for supplied flow data; no existence or global-flow theorem is asserted.
items.strategy:
1.1 For each component $\chi_i$, joint $C^2$ regularity and [F1] give $\partial_t\partial_{a_j}\chi_i=\partial_{a_j}\partial_t\chi_i$. Differentiating the given velocity equation in $a$ and applying [F2] yields $\partial_tF=LF$, where $L(t,a):=(D_xb)(t,\chi(t,a))$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Each $F(t,a)$ is invertible: differentiating $\chi_t^{-1}\circ\chi_t=\operatorname{id}$ by [F2] gives $D\chi_t^{-1}(\chi_t(a))F(t,a)=I$. Thus [F3] applies to the $C^1$ matrix curve $t\mapsto F(t,a)$ and gives $\partial_tJ=J\operatorname{tr}(F^{-1}LF)$. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 By [F4], $\operatorname{tr}(F^{-1}LF)=\operatorname{tr}(FF^{-1}L)=\operatorname{tr}L=\sum_i\partial_{x_i}b_i(t,\chi(t,a))$. Also $F(0,a)=I$, so $J(0,a)=1$. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The determinant $J(t,a)$ is continuous and nonzero on $I$ by step 2.1. If it were negative for some $t$, [F6] on the closed segment with endpoints $0$ and $t$ would give a point where $J=0$, contradicting invertibility. Hence $J>0$. [given, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1]

4.2 If $\operatorname{div}b=0$, step 3.1 gives $\partial_tJ=0$. For each fixed $a$, the case $t=0$ is already $J(0,a)=1$. For $t\ne0$, apply [F5] to $J(\cdot,a)$ on $[\min(0,t),\max(0,t)]$, whose endpoints are distinct; since its derivative is zero, its endpoint difference is zero, so $J(t,a)=J(0,a)=1$. [given, F5, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For the torus clause, fix $a\in\mathbb T^n$ and $t_0\in I$. By continuity, choose a time neighborhood of $t_0$ on which $a$ and $\chi_t(a)$ stay in translation charts. Their transition maps are translations, so the coordinate matrices of $D_a\chi_t$, their determinants, and the coordinate divergence of $b$ agree on overlaps. In these charts the Euclidean calculations in steps 1.1–3.1 prove both differential identities, and $\chi_0=\operatorname{id}$ gives $J(0,a)=1$. Since $t_0$ was arbitrary, the identities hold throughout $I$; applying steps 4.1 and 4.2 on the closed segment between $0$ and any $t\in I$ gives positivity and the divergence-free conclusion. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2] ∎

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Introduction to Analysis in Several Variables (Advanced Calculus), §§2.1–2.3
Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th edition, Theorem 8.49

items.title: Fine entropy under a specified incompressible periodic flow
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement: Use $\log$ for the natural logarithm of [[def-natural-logarithm]]. Let $\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\Lambda$ be a flat translation torus, where $\Lambda=\mathbb Z\ell_1+\cdots+\mathbb Z\ell_n$ for a linearly independent basis $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n$, with the smooth structure and Euclidean metric descended from $\mathbb R^n$. Let $\mu=c\,da$ be its fixed translation-invariant volume measure in dimensionless translation coordinates, with $c>0$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$. Suppose $\chi:I\times\mathbb T^n\to\mathbb T^n$ is jointly $C^2$, each $\chi_t$ is a diffeomorphism, and $\chi_0=\operatorname{id}$. Let $\pi:T\mathbb T^n\to\mathbb T^n$ be the tangent-bundle projection and let $b:I\times\mathbb T^n\to T\mathbb T^n$ have $C^1$ chart coefficients with $\pi(b(t,a))=a$ and $\partial_t\chi(t,a)=b(t,\chi(t,a))$. In translation charts write $b=\sum_i b^i\partial_{x^i}$ and define $\operatorname{div}b=\sum_i\partial_{x^i}b^i$. Assume $\operatorname{div}b=0$ in these charts. Let $f_0\in C^1(\mathbb T^n)$ satisfy $0<m\le f_0\le M<\infty$ and $\int f_0\,d\mu=1$, and define $f_t:=f_0\circ\chi_t^{-1}$. Then $f_t$ is a probability density for every $t\in I$, the integral $H(f_t):=-\int_{\mathbb T^n}f_t\log f_t\,d\mu$ is finite, and $H(f_t)=H(f_0)$. Here $H$ is the dimensionless fine entropy of this density; multiplication by a physical constant such as $k_B$ is a separate interpretation.
items.strategy:
1.1 Apply [F1] to the given family. Its hypotheses are exactly the supplied $C^2$ diffeomorphisms, identity initial map and $C^1$ divergence-free velocity, so every local translation-chart Jacobian is $J_t=1$. [given, F1]



2.1 For fixed $t$, around each point choose a source chart and a smaller coordinate neighborhood whose closure maps under $\chi_t$ into a target chart. Continuity and compactness give finitely many closed coordinate boxes $Q_j$ with interiors covering the torus and with each $\chi_t(Q_j)$ inside a target chart. Put $E_1=Q_1$ and $E_j=Q_j\setminus\bigcup_{i<j}\operatorname{int}(Q_i)$; each $E_j$ is compact, the pieces cover the torus, and any overlap lies on one of the box faces. Each $E_j$ is Jordan because its boundary lies in a finite union of coordinate faces, which are compact $C^1$ hypersurface patches. A $C^1$ graph patch has bounded slope on a compact subpatch, so its mesh-$h$ box cover has total $n$-volume $O(h)$ and hence content zero. On compact chart neighborhoods $\chi_t$ has bounded derivative, so it maps these zero-content boundaries to zero-content boundaries. Each compact piece and its image therefore have Jordan boundaries and lie in source and target charts; [F2] applies there. Summing over the pieces, overlaps do not affect the integrals, translation chart changes preserve $da$, and the constant $c$ is the same on both sides. Thus for every continuous $\varphi$ on the torus, $\int\varphi\circ\chi_t\,d\mu=\int\varphi J_t\,d\mu=\int\varphi\,d\mu$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1]



3.1 The function $f_t=f_0\circ\chi_t^{-1}$ is positive and continuous. The substitution of step 2.1 with $\varphi=f_t$ gives $\int f_t\,d\mu=\int f_0\,d\mu=1$, so $f_t$ is normalized. [given, step 2.1]



4.1 The bounds $m\le f_0\le M$ also hold for $f_t$; by [F3], $\log$ is continuous on $[m,M]$, so $f_t\log f_t$ is bounded and continuous on the compact torus and its integral is finite. Applying step 2.1 to $\varphi=f_t\log f_t$ gives $\int f_t\log f_t\,d\mu=\int (f_t\log f_t)\circ\chi_t\,d\mu=\int f_0\log f_0\,d\mu$, since $f_t\circ\chi_t=f_0$. Negating proves $H(f_t)=H(f_0)$. [given, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Introduction to Analysis in Several Variables (Advanced Calculus), §3.1 and Chapter 4, §4.5
David Tong, Statistical Physics, §1.2, entropy as a functional of a specified state

items.title: Gaussian covariance for positive quadratic forms and a boundary counterexample
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined in [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $n\ge1$, let $K\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive definite, and let $\beta>0$. For $x\in\mathbb R^n$ put $H(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Kx$, and use the Euclidean Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n$ to define the density $Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H(x)}$. Then

$$Z=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\beta H(x)}dx=\left(\frac{2\pi}{\beta}\right)^{n/2}(\det K)^{-1/2},\quad \mathbb E[x]=0,\quad \mathbb E[xx^{\mathsf T}]=\beta^{-1}K^{-1},\quad \mathbb E[H]=\frac{n}{2\beta}.$$

Positive definiteness and $\beta>0$ are essential for this normalized full-space Gaussian. The unrestricted identity $\mathbb E[x\,H'(x)]=\beta^{-1}$ is false without a boundary hypothesis: on $[-L,L]$ with $L>0$ and $H\equiv0$, the normalized expectation on the left is $0$.
items.strategy:
1.1 We construct $R$ with $K=R^{\mathsf T}R$ by induction on $n$. For $n=1$, take $R=\sqrt{K_{11}}>0$. For $n>1$, write $K=\begin{pmatrix}a&b^{\mathsf T}\\b&C\end{pmatrix}$; positive definiteness gives $a>0$ and $S:=C-bb^{\mathsf T}/a$ positive definite, since $y^{\mathsf T}Sy=(-b^{\mathsf T}y/a,y)^{\mathsf T}K(-b^{\mathsf T}y/a,y)>0$ for $y\ne0$. By induction $S=R_1^{\mathsf T}R_1$; then $R=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt a&b^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt a\\0&R_1\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $R^{\mathsf T}R=K$. Its diagonal entries are positive, so $\det R>0$; taking determinants gives $\det K=(\det R)^2$ and therefore $\det R=\sqrt{\det K}$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Put $T(x)=Rx$. This is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^n$ with $|\det DT|=\det R$. Since $H(x)=|Rx|^2/2$, [F2] gives $$Z=(\det R)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\beta|y|^2/2}\,d\lambda_n(y).$$ By [F3], $\lambda_n$ is the finite product of $n$ sigma-finite one-dimensional Lebesgue measures; Tonelli and the factorization $e^{-\beta|y|^2/2}=\prod_i e^{-\beta y_i^2/2}$ give the integral as $I_0(\beta/2)^n$. By [F1] and [F4], $I_0(\beta/2)=\sqrt{2\pi/\beta}$. Hence $$Z=(2\pi/\beta)^{n/2}(\det K)^{-1/2},$$ which is finite and positive. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $Y$ have the normalized density proportional to $e^{-\beta|y|^2/2}$ with respect to $\lambda_n$. For each $i$, [F3] and Tonelli factor the nonnegative second-moment integral into $I_1(\beta/2)I_0(\beta/2)^{n-1}$, while the normalizer is $I_0(\beta/2)^n$; [F1] gives $\mathbb E[Y_i^2]=I_1(\beta/2)/I_0(\beta/2)=1/\beta$. Also $\int |y_i|e^{-\beta|y|^2/2}d\lambda_n<\infty$, since $|y_i|\le1+y_i^2$ and the same Tonelli factorization makes both integrals finite. For $i\ne j$, $|y_iy_j|\le(y_i^2+y_j^2)/2$, so the cross moments are absolutely integrable. Fubini [F3] factors these signed moments; the one-dimensional first and odd moments vanish by [F1]. Thus $\mathbb E[Y]=0$ and $\mathbb E[YY^{\mathsf T}]=\beta^{-1}I$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F2], the normalized law of $X$ is the pullback of the law of $Y$ under $x=R^{-1}y$. The absolute integrability established in step 3.1 permits the same change of variables for signed first and second moments by applying [F2] to their positive and negative parts. Hence $\mathbb E[X]=0$ and $$\mathbb E[XX^{\mathsf T}]=R^{-1}(\beta^{-1}I)R^{-\mathsf T}=\beta^{-1}(R^{\mathsf T}R)^{-1}=\beta^{-1}K^{-1}.$$ Since $H(X)=|Y|^2/2$, summing the diagonal second moments gives $\mathbb E[H]=n/(2\beta)$. [F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For the stated boundary counterexample, the density on $[-L,L]$ is the constant $(2L)^{-1}$ because $H=0$ and the normalizing integral is $2L$ by [F3]. Since $H'(x)=0$ everywhere, $\mathbb E[xH'(x)]=0\ne\beta^{-1}$ for $\beta>0$. [given, F3, algebra] ∎

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Introduction to Analysis in Several Variables (Advanced Calculus), §3.1
David Tong, Statistical Physics, §2.2.1, equipartition of quadratic degrees of freedom

items.title: Exact spherical-shell coordinate marginal and fixed-block Gaussian limit
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined in [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $D\ge2$, $1\le k<D$, and $R>0$. Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_D$ be independent real random variables with common Lebesgue probability density $\phi(x):=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$; its integral is one by the Gaussian integral in [[lem-csm-examples-gamma-gaussian-tools]], and this is the standard-normal coordinate law. Set $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_D)$ and define $P:=RZ/|Z|$ when $Z\ne0$, and $P:=0$ when $Z=0$. The joint density of $Z$ makes $\mathbb P(Z=0)=0$. The distribution of $P$ is rotationally invariant, meaning that for every orthogonal map $Q\in O(D)$ and Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^D$, $\mathbb P(QP\in A)=\mathbb P(P\in A)$. It is concentrated on the sphere in the precise sense that $\mathbb P(|P|=R)=1$. Its first $k$ coordinates have Lebesgue density

$$f_{D,k}(y)=\frac{\Gamma(D/2)}{\Gamma((D-k)/2)(\pi R^2)^{k/2}}\left(1-\frac{|y|^2}{R^2}\right)^{(D-k-2)/2}\quad (|y|<R),$$

and zero for $|y|\ge R$. This density is integrable even when it diverges at the boundary. Also $\mathbb E[P_i]=0$, $\mathbb E[P_iP_j]=0$ for $i\ne j$, and $\mathbb E[P_i^2]=R^2/D$.

For fixed $k$ and $\sigma>0$, set $R_D=\sqrt D\,\sigma$ and let $D\to\infty$ through integers $D>k$. If $g:\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R$ is bounded and Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm, meaning that finite constants $B_g,L_g$ satisfy $|g(x)|\le B_g$ and $|g(x)-g(y)|\le L_g|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^k$, then

$$\mathbb E\,g\bigl((P_1,\ldots,P_k)\bigr)\longrightarrow\mathbb E\,g\bigl(\sigma(Z_1,\ldots,Z_k)\bigr).$$

This is a fixed-block bounded-Lipschitz test limit; it makes no claim uniform in $k$ or for unbounded test functions. If $k=D$, the projection is singular on the sphere and the displayed Lebesgue density is not asserted.
items.strategy:
1.1 The joint density of $Z$ is $(2\pi)^{-D/2}e^{-|z|^2/2}$. For every orthogonal $Q$, the substitution $z\mapsto Qz$ has absolute determinant $1$ and preserves $|z|$, so $QZ$ has the same law as $Z$. Therefore $P=RZ/|Z|$ is rotationally invariant and satisfies $|P|=R$ almost surely. [given, F1, F2, algebra]



1.2 Write $Z=(A,B)$ with $A\in\mathbb R^k$ and $B\in\mathbb R^{D-k}$. The vectors are independent. By the one-coordinate substitution $w=Z_j^2/2$, each $w$ has gamma density $w^{-1/2}e^{-w}/\Gamma(1/2)$; repeated application of [F1] shows $T:=|B|^2$ has density $t^{b-1}e^{-t/2}/(2^b\Gamma(b))$ for $t>0$, where $b=(D-k)/2$, independently of $A$. [F1, algebra]



1.3 For fixed $t>0$, the first $k$ coordinates $y=RA/\sqrt{|A|^2+t}$ range over $|y|<R$. The inverse is $A=\sqrt t\,y/\sqrt{R^2-|y|^2}$. Its derivative has radial eigenvalue $\sqrt t\,R^2/(R^2-|y|^2)^{3/2}$ and $k-1$ tangential eigenvalues $\sqrt t/(R^2-|y|^2)^{1/2}$, hence Jacobian $t^{k/2}R^2/(R^2-|y|^2)^{k/2+1}$. [given, construct, algebra]



2.1 The map $(y,t)\mapsto(A(y,t),t)$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism from $\{|y|<R,t>0\}$ to $\mathbb R^k\times(0,\infty)$. Apply [F2] first on compact subsets away from $t=0$ and $|y|=R$ and then take increasing nonnegative limits. Substituting the Gaussian density of $A$, the gamma density of $T$, and the Jacobian from step 1.3 gives $f_{D,k}(y)=\frac{R^2}{(2\pi)^{k/2}2^b\Gamma(b)(R^2-|y|^2)^{k/2+1}}\int_0^\infty t^{D/2-1}\exp\!\left(-\frac{tR^2}{2(R^2-|y|^2)}\right)dt$. The substitution $u=tR^2/[2(R^2-|y|^2)]$ evaluates the integral as $\Gamma(D/2)[2(R^2-|y|^2)/R^2]^{D/2}$. Since $D/2=k/2+b$, simplification gives the displayed density. The boundary singularity, when present, has exponent $b-1>-1$ in the radial variable and is integrable; the pushforward construction and $\mathbb P(Z=0)=0$ show the density has total mass one and no boundary atom. [F1, F2, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]



2.2 Sign changes of one Gaussian coordinate show $\mathbb E[P_i]=0$ and $\mathbb E[P_iP_j]=0$ for $i\ne j$. Permutation invariance makes all $\mathbb E[P_i^2]$ equal, while $\sum_{i=1}^D P_i^2=R^2$ almost surely; summing expectations gives $\mathbb E[P_i^2]=R^2/D$. [step 1.1, given, algebra]



3.1 For each finite $D$, take the product Gaussian vector $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_D)$ in that dimension and set $S_D:=D^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^D Z_i^2$. By [F1] and independence, $\mathbb E S_D=1$, $\mathbb E[(S_D-1)^2]=2/D$, and $\mathbb E|Z_{1:k}|^2=k$. Fix $0<\delta<1/2$ and $M>0$. On $E_D=\{|Z_{1:k}|\le M,\ |S_D-1|\le\delta\}$, the derivative of $u^{-1/2}$ is bounded by $\sqrt2$ on $[1/2,3/2]$, so $|\sigma Z_{1:k}/\sqrt{S_D}-\sigma Z_{1:k}|\le\sqrt2\sigma M\delta$. If $g$ is bounded Lipschitz with bound $B_g$ and Lipschitz constant $L_g$, then $M^2\mathbf 1_{\{|Z_{1:k}|>M\}}\le |Z_{1:k}|^2$ and $\delta^2\mathbf 1_{\{|S_D-1|>\delta\}}\le(S_D-1)^2$ imply $\mathbb P(E_D^c)\le k/M^2+2/(D\delta^2)$. Therefore $|\mathbb E g(P_{1:k})-\mathbb E g(\sigma Z_{1:k})|\le L_g\sqrt2\sigma M\delta+2B_g\left(\frac{k}{M^2}+\frac{2}{D\delta^2}\right)$. Choose $M$ large, then $\delta$ small, then $D$ large. The right side becomes arbitrarily small, proving the stated test convergence without assuming independence between $Z_{1:k}$ and $S_D$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

Here $\log$ denotes the natural logarithm defined in [[def-natural-logarithm]].

For each named finite classical model in this page, adopt the preparation explicitly stated in its theorem. In a canonical branch, take a measurable phase space with a specified reference measure $\nu$, a measurable Hamiltonian $H$, an inverse energy parameter $\beta>0$, and a finite positive partition function $Z=\int e^{-\beta H}\,d\nu$; the adopted probability measure is $dP=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H}\,d\nu$. In a grand-canonical branch, take disjoint particle-number sectors with sector partition functions $Z_N$ and a dimensionless activity $z>0$ for which $\Xi=\sum_{N\ge0}z^N Z_N$ is finite; sector $N$ has probability weight $z^N Z_N/\Xi$. The spherical-shell and product preparations are separate explicitly specified probability laws in their consuming theorem statements. These are alternative model assumptions, not consequences of a Hamiltonian flow and not assertions that a laboratory system realizes them.

For a canonical model whose reference measure and Hamiltonian are fixed, adopt the statistical thermodynamic definitions $U=\mathbb E_P[H]$, $F=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$, and $S=k_B(\log Z+\beta U)$ when the displayed integrals are finite. For a volume-dependent model, define the model pressure as $-\partial_V F$ only along the declared fixed-shape volume family. Here $k_B>0$ has SI units J K$^{-1}$, temperature $T>0$ has units K, and $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ has units J$^{-1}$. The fixed reference measure is part of the preparation; changing it changes the numerical partition function and entropy convention.

For the continuous particle examples, adopt the operational species and
counting convention of [[post-csm-counting-and-physical-observables]]. Use
one fixed primitive action reference $a_0>0$ in J s, and write $h_0:=a_0$
where the consuming model uses the notation $h_0$. In a Cartesian physical
phase chart $dq\,dp$ has action dimension $(\mathrm{J\,s})^{dN}$, so the
reference $dq\,dp/(\prod_sN_s!\,a_0^{dN})$ is dimensionless. Each model
retains its declared operational labels: an omitted factorial for resolved
harmonic coordinates is not replaced by a particle-exchange quotient. The
finite spin examples use their stated discrete counting measure, without a
continuous phase-cell factor. Choosing a numerical reference action, or
identifying it with Planck's constant, is an additional convention; no such
value or identification is imposed here. The Gaussian and gamma identities
in [[lem-csm-examples-gamma-gaussian-tools]] establish the mathematical
normalizations, not the physical preparation or empirical equilibration.

items.title: Confined coupled quadratic canonical systems
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined in [[def-countable-choice]] for the Euclidean Lebesgue product measure used below. Let $n\ge1$, let $M=\operatorname{diag}(m_1,\ldots,m_n)$ with $m_i>0$ in kg, and let $K$ be a real symmetric positive-definite stiffness matrix with entries in J m$^{-2}$. For displacement $q\in\mathbb R^n$ in metres and momentum $p\in\mathbb R^n$ in kg m s$^{-1}$, define
$$H(q,p)=\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}p+\tfrac12q^{\mathsf T}Kq.$$
Adopt the canonical probability density proportional to $e^{-\beta H}$ relative to $dq\,dp/h_0^n$, where $\beta>0$ has units J$^{-1}$ and the fixed action reference $h_0>0$ has units J s. Under the preparation of [[post-csm-examples-ensemble-preparations]], the dimensionless partition function and moments are
$$Z=\left(\frac{2\pi}{\beta h_0}\right)^n\sqrt{\frac{\det M}{\det K}},\quad \mathbb E[q]=\mathbb E[p]=0,\quad \mathbb E[qq^{\mathsf T}]=\beta^{-1}K^{-1},\quad \mathbb E[pp^{\mathsf T}]=\beta^{-1}M,\quad \mathbb E[qp^{\mathsf T}]=0.$$
The model mean energy is $U=\mathbb E[H]=n/\beta$. With $k_B>0$ in J K$^{-1}$ and $T>0$ in K from [[post-csm-examples-ensemble-preparations]], so that $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, define the fixed-parameter heat-capacity response by
$$C_{\mathrm{harm}}:=\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_{M,K,h_0}=nk_B.$$
It has units J K$^{-1}$. This model has no volume variable, so $C_{\mathrm{harm}}$ is not a fixed-volume derivative.
items.strategy:
1.1 By [F1], the phase-space weight factors as $e^{-\beta p^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}p/2}e^{-\beta q^{\mathsf T}Kq/2}$. The product-measure identity and Tonelli [F3] justify multiplying the two nonnegative Lebesgue integrals. Applying [F2] to the $q$ factor gives normalization $(2\pi/\beta)^{n/2}(\det K)^{-1/2}$ and covariance $\beta^{-1}K^{-1}$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]



1.2 The momentum quadratic form has symmetric positive-definite matrix $M^{-1}$. Applying [F2] with $K=M^{-1}$ gives its integral $(2\pi/\beta)^{n/2}\sqrt{\det M}$ and covariance of $p$ equal to $\beta^{-1}(M^{-1})^{-1}=\beta^{-1}M$. [given, F2, algebra]



2.1 Multiplying the two integrals from steps 1.1–1.2 and dividing by the reference factor $h_0^n$ gives $Z=(2\pi/(\beta h_0))^n\sqrt{\det M/\det K}$. The phase-space Lebesgue measure is the product of its $q$ and $p$ factors by [F3]; the normalized canonical density therefore factors into independent $q$ and $p$ laws. Each factor is even, so its mean is zero, and its covariance is the one computed in steps 1.1–1.2. [A1, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]



3.1 By [F1], taking the expectation of $H$ and summing the diagonal traces of the two covariance identities gives $$U=\tfrac12\mathbb E[p^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}p]+\tfrac12\mathbb E[q^{\mathsf T}Kq]=\frac{n}{2\beta}+\frac{n}{2\beta}=\frac{n}{\beta}.$$ The adopted relation $\beta^{-1}=k_BT$ makes $U=nk_BT$. Holding the model parameters $M,K,h_0$ fixed therefore gives $C_{\mathrm{harm}}=(\partial U/\partial T)_{M,K,h_0}=nk_B$, with units J K$^{-1}$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

items.title: Exact canonical and grand ideal-gas preparations
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined in [[def-countable-choice]], for the Euclidean Lebesgue product and polar-coordinate suppliers used below. Let $\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n/n!$ be the real exponential of [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], and let $\log$ be the natural logarithm of [[def-natural-logarithm]], with $\log'(x)=1/x$ for $x>0$ by [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]. Let $d,N\ge1$ and let $B=\prod_{j=1}^d[0,L_j]\subset\mathbb R^d$, where each side length $L_j>0$ is in metres and $V:=\prod_jL_j$ is in $\mathrm m^d$. Let $m>0$ be the common particle mass in kg, $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$, and let $h_0:=a_0>0$ be the fixed action reference in J s from [[post-csm-examples-ensemble-preparations]]. Take one species of $N$ operationally indistinguishable particles as in [[post-csm-counting-and-physical-observables]]. On its auxiliary labelled cover, positions $q_i\in B$ are in metres and momenta $p_i\in\mathbb R^d$ are in kg m s$^{-1}$; the Hamiltonian is permutation invariant and the reference measure is
$$d\nu_N=\frac{dq\,dp}{N!h_0^{dN}}.$$
The symmetric labelled law represents the quotient preparation; a one-particle marginal below means the law of a uniformly selected particle. For $N\ge1$, define
$$H_N(q,p)=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{|p_i|^2}{2m}$$
and use the canonical preparation of [[post-csm-examples-ensemble-preparations]]. For the vacuum sector $N=0$, define $B^0\times\mathbb R^{d\cdot0}$ to be a singleton with reference measure $\nu_0=1$, set $H_0=0$, and use empty-product conventions $V^0=0!=h_0^0=1$; thus $Z_0=1$. The mass parameter $m$ applies when particles are present; the vacuum sector has no mass coordinate. For all $N\ge0$, set $\lambda:=h_0\sqrt{\beta/(2\pi m)}$ (metres) and
$$Z_N=\int e^{-\beta H_N}\,d\nu_N=\frac{V^N}{N!\lambda^{dN}}.$$
For $N\ge1$, the labelled-cover position coordinates are independent uniform points of $B$ and are independent of the momenta; all momentum components are independent centered Gaussians of variance $m/\beta$. The joint law is permutation invariant. The energy satisfies $U=\mathbb E H_N=dN/(2\beta)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(H_N)=dN/(2\beta^2)$, with variance in J$^2$. With the adopted Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in J K$^{-1}$ and temperature $T:=(k_B\beta)^{-1}>0$ in K from [[post-csm-examples-ensemble-preparations]], define $F=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_N$ and scale all box side lengths uniformly when varying $V$, holding the shape, $N,T,d,m,h_0$ fixed. The model pressure $\mathcal P:=-\left(\partial F/\partial V\right)_{N,T,d,m,h_0,\,\mathrm{shape}}$ has units J m$^{-d}$ (equivalently N m$^{1-d}$; Pa when $d=3$) and obeys $\mathcal PV=N/\beta=Nk_BT$. The fixed-reference entropy is $S=k_B(\log Z_N+\beta U)$ and retains the chosen $N!$ and $h_0$ convention.

For $d=3$, the speed $v=|p|/m$ of a uniformly selected particle, in m s$^{-1}$, has density
$$f(v)=4\pi\left(\frac{m\beta}{2\pi}\right)^{3/2}v^2e^{-\beta mv^2/2},\qquad v\ge0.$$
Its squared-speed expectation, modal speed, and mean speed are $\mathbb E[v^2]=3/(m\beta)$ in m$^2$ s$^{-2}$, $\sqrt{2/(m\beta)}$ in m s$^{-1}$, and $\mathbb E[v]=\sqrt{8/(\pi m\beta)}$ in m s$^{-1}$, respectively.

For the separate grand-canonical preparation of [[post-csm-examples-ensemble-preparations]] on disjoint number sectors $N\in\{0,1,\ldots\}$, whose sector weights are proportional to $z^NZ_N$, let $\mu_{\rm chem}$ be a chemical potential in joules and $z=\exp(\beta\mu_{\rm chem})>0$ the dimensionless activity. Then
$$\Xi=\sum_{N=0}^\infty z^NZ_N=\exp(zV/\lambda^d),\qquad \mathbb P(N=j)=\exp(-\nu)\frac{\nu^j}{j!},\quad \nu:=zV/\lambda^d,$$
so $\mathbb E N=\operatorname{Var}(N)=\nu$ and the conditional law given $N$ is the canonical law above.

A distinct three-dimensional classical ultra-relativistic model adopts $H_{\rm ur}(p)=c|p|$ for every $p\in\mathbb R^3$, with $c>0$ in m s$^{-1}$ and $p$ in kg m s$^{-1}$, in the same box volume $V$ in m$^3$. This extends the nonzero massless momentum formula continuously to $p=0$ only to define a density on all of $\mathbb R^3$; the point has Lebesgue measure zero and no physical zero-momentum massless state is asserted. Its separate canonical partition function is
$$Z_{N,{\rm ur}}=\frac{V^N}{N!h_0^{3N}}\left(\frac{8\pi}{(\beta c)^3}\right)^N,$$
with $U_{\rm ur}=3N/\beta$ J and $\operatorname{Var}(H_{\rm ur})=3N/\beta^2$ J$^2$. Define its fixed-volume heat capacity by $C_{V,\rm ur}:=(\partial U_{\rm ur}/\partial T)_{V,N,c,h_0}=3Nk_B$; it has units J K$^{-1}$. Its three-dimensional pressure obeys $\mathcal PV=N/\beta$ and has units Pa. This branch is not obtained by setting $m=0$ in the Gaussian model and makes no photon-number or quantum-statistics claim.
items.strategy:
**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $d,N\ge1$, the rectangular box $B$ with side lengths in metres and volume $V$ in $\mathrm m^d$, one operationally indistinguishable species, $m>0$ kg, $h_0=a_0>0$ J s, $\beta>0$ J$^{-1}$, and the Hamiltonian and symmetric reference measure in the Statement.

1.1 By [F3], Euclidean Lebesgue measure in the position and momentum coordinates is their product measure; [F5] then factors the nonnegative normalization integral. The box-volume formula [F4] gives $\lambda_{dN}(B^N)=V^N$. Each of the $dN$ scalar momentum factors contributes $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-\beta p^2/(2m)}dp=\sqrt{2\pi m/\beta}$ by [F2] and [F7]. Including the stipulated factor $1/(N!h_0^{dN})$ from [F12] yields $Z_N=V^N(N!h_0^{dN})^{-1}(2\pi m/\beta)^{dN/2}=V^N/(N!\lambda^{dN})$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F7, F12, algebra]

1.2 For the separate massless branch, let $N_{\rm time}$ denote the background's smooth future-timelike field $N$ from [F10] and normalize it at the event by $n=N_{\rm time}/\sqrt{-g(N_{\rm time},N_{\rm time})}$. [F8] makes $P$ future null, so $g(P,n)<0$. By [F11], $|q_n(P)|^2=g(q_n(P),q_n(P))=g(P,n)^2$, hence $E_n(P)=-cg(P,n)=c|q_n(P)|$. Identifying $q_n$ with its components in an orthonormal basis of the positive rest space gives the adopted $H_{\rm ur}(p)=c|p|$ with the stated units. [given, A2, F8, F9, F10, F11, algebra]

2.1 After normalization, the canonical density is the product of the uniform position density on $B^N$ and the $dN$ scalar Gaussian momentum densities. For measurable coordinate rectangles, [F3] and [F5] show their probabilities factor; hence the positions and all momentum components are independent, each position is uniform on $B$, and each momentum component is centered with variance $m/\beta$ by [F2]. [given, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1]

2.2 In the grand preparation of [F1], use the vacuum convention $Z_0=1$ and substitute $Z_N=V^N/(N!\lambda^{dN})$ for all $N\ge0$ into the sector sum. With $\nu=zV/\lambda^d$, [F13] gives $\Xi=\sum_{N\ge0}\nu^N/N!=\exp(\nu)$, and [F14] gives the normalized sector weight $\nu^N/(N!\exp(\nu))=\exp(-\nu)\nu^N/N!$. [A1, F1, F13, F14, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 By [F6], the momentum integral for one ultra-relativistic particle is $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-\beta c|p|}\,d\lambda_3(p)=4\pi\int_0^\infty r^2e^{-\beta cr}dr=4\pi\frac{\Gamma(3)}{(\beta c)^3}=\frac{8\pi}{(\beta c)^3},$$ using [F2]. The point $p=0$ is Lebesgue null by [F18], so the continuous extension adds no massless zero-momentum state. Product measure and Tonelli [F3, F5] give the $N$-particle product, and the stated positional/counting reference then gives $Z_{N,\rm ur}$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F18, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Each scalar momentum coordinate has second moment $m/\beta$ and fourth moment $3m^2/\beta^2$ from [F2]. Thus each term $p_{i\alpha}^2/(2m)$ has mean $1/(2\beta)$ and variance $1/(2\beta^2)$; independence from step 2.1 makes means and variances add, giving the stated $U$ and $\operatorname{Var}(H_N)$. [given, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 For $d=3$, write $a=\beta/(2m)$. The one-particle momentum density is $(a/\pi)^{3/2}e^{-a|p|^2}$. By [F6], for every Borel $A\subseteq[0,\infty)$ the probability that $v=|p|/m$ lies in $A$ is $$4\pi(a/\pi)^{3/2}\int_{mA}r^2e^{-ar^2}\,dr.$$ The substitution $r=mv$ therefore gives the speed density $4\pi(m\beta/(2\pi))^{3/2}v^2e^{-\beta mv^2/2}$ on $v\ge0$. [given, F2, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

3.3 Shifting the index in the absolutely convergent series [F13] gives $\sum_{j\ge0}j\nu^j/j!=\nu\exp(\nu)$ and $\sum_{j\ge0}j(j-1)\nu^j/j!=\nu^2\exp(\nu)$. After normalization by [F14], $\mathbb E N=\nu$ and $\mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\nu^2$, hence $\operatorname{Var}(N)=\mathbb E[N(N-1)]+\mathbb EN-(\mathbb EN)^2=\nu$. Conditioning on sector $N$ recovers the canonical density because its factor $z^N$ is constant within that sector. [F13, F14, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 By [F17] and [A1], $F=-\beta^{-1}[N\log(V/\lambda^d)-\log N!]$ for fixed $T,N$ and fixed box shape. The log derivative [F16] gives $-\partial_VF=N/(\beta V)$, with $\mathcal P$ in J m$^{-d}$, and therefore $\mathcal PV=N/\beta$. The entropy definition in [F1] gives $S=k_B(\log Z_N+\beta U)$ with the same fixed $h_0$ and factorial convention. [A1, F1, F15, F16, F17, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 The speed density is proportional to $v^2e^{-av^2}$ with $a=\beta m/2$. Its derivative has the sign of $2v(1-av^2)$ for $v>0$, so its unique positive maximum occurs at $v_{\rm mode}=a^{-1/2}$. The second moment is $3/(2a)=3/(m\beta)$ by the gamma recurrence in [F2]. The mean is $$\mathbb E v=\frac{4a^{3/2}}{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^\infty v^3e^{-av^2}dv=\frac{4a^{3/2}}{\sqrt\pi}\frac{\Gamma(2)}{2a^2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi a}}=\sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi\beta m}}.$$ These are model-distribution moments, not values for an individual measured particle. [F2, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 Under the normalized radial density proportional to $r^2e^{-\beta cr}$, gamma moments give mean energy $3/\beta$ and variance $3/\beta^2$ per particle. Independence from the product preparation adds these to $U_{\rm ur}=3N/\beta$ and $\operatorname{Var}(H_{\rm ur})=3N/\beta^2$; differentiating at fixed $V,N,c,h_0$ with $\beta^{-1}=k_BT$ gives $C_{V,\rm ur}=3Nk_B$ J K$^{-1}$. Since $Z_{N,\rm ur}$ is proportional to $V^N$, [F16] gives $-\partial_VF=N/(\beta V)$ and $\mathcal PV=N/\beta$, with $\mathcal P$ in Pa for this three-dimensional branch. [A1, F1, F2, F5, F16, step 2.3, algebra] ∎

items.title: Finite periodic Ising-ring correlations and exact decay
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Use the real exponential $\exp(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/n!$ of [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and the hyperbolic functions $\cosh x=(\exp x+\exp(-x))/2$, $\sinh x=(\exp x-\exp(-x))/2$. Define $\tanh x:=\sinh x/\cosh x$; the denominator is positive for every real $x$. Let $N\ge2$, let $\Omega_N=\{-1,1\}^N$ with cyclic indexing $s_{N+1}=s_1$, and count exactly the $N$ indexed periodic bonds (so $N=2$ has two bonds). For coupling $J\ge0$ in joules, zero field, and $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$, adopt the finite canonical law
$$\mathbb P_N(s)=Z_N^{-1}\exp\!\left(\beta J\sum_{i=1}^Ns_is_{i+1}\right).$$
Set $t=\tanh(\beta J)\in[0,1)$. For $1\le r\le N-1$,
$$\mathbb E_N[s_i]=0,\qquad \mathbb E_N[s_i s_{i+r}]=\frac{t^r+t^{N-r}}{1+t^N}.$$
For each fixed positive integer separation $r$ and $N\to\infty$, the correlation tends to $t^r$, with absolute error at most $t^{N-r}+t^{N+r}$. When $J>0$, define the limiting correlation length $\xi>0$ in lattice spacings as the unique number satisfying $t^r=e^{-r/\xi}$ for every positive integer separation $r$; equivalently, $\xi=-1/\log t$. The zero-field susceptibility per spin, defined by $\chi_N:=N^{-1}\partial_h\mathbb E_{N,h}[\sum_i s_i]|_{h=0}$ for the field-coupled law with energy $-\!J\sum_i s_is_{i+1}-h\sum_i s_i$, where the field parameter $h\in\mathbb R$ is in joules, has limit
$$\chi_\infty=\beta\frac{1+t}{1-t}.$$
Both $\chi_N$ and $\chi_\infty$ have units J$^{-1}$ per spin (the spin variables are dimensionless).
Define the finite-ring model free energy by $F_N:=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_N$ and its limiting free energy per spin, when the limit exists, by $f_\infty:=\lim_{N\to\infty}F_N/N$. Then $f_\infty=-\beta^{-1}\log(2\cosh(\beta J))$, analytic at every finite positive temperature. No statement is made for arbitrary one-dimensional interactions.
items.strategy:
1.1 In the zero-field case the transfer matrix in [F2] is $T_{s,t}=e^{Kst}$ with $K=\beta J$, so $T=\begin{pmatrix}e^K&e^{-K}\\e^{-K}&e^K\end{pmatrix}$. Direct multiplication gives orthonormal eigenvectors $u_+=(1,1)/\sqrt2$, $u_-=(1,-1)/\sqrt2$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_+=2\cosh K$ and $\lambda_-=2\sinh K$. Hence $Z_N=\operatorname{tr}(T^N)=\lambda_+^N+\lambda_-^N=\lambda_+^N(1+t^N)$, where $t=\lambda_-/\lambda_+=\tanh K$. [given, F2, algebra]



2.1 By the finite preparation [F1], the partition sum is the normalization for the adopted law. Put $D_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$; then $D_0u_+=u_-$ and $D_0u_-=u_+$. Expanding the finite canonical sum over the $N$ cyclic indices with $s_i s_{i+r}$ inserted gives numerator $\operatorname{tr}(D_0T^rD_0T^{N-r})$. Evaluating this trace in the eigenbasis yields $\lambda_-^r\lambda_+^{N-r}+\lambda_+^r\lambda_-^{N-r}$. Dividing by $Z_N$ from step 1.1 gives the stated correlation formula. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]



3.1 The map $s\mapsto-s$ preserves every bond product and reverses $\sum_i s_i$, so at zero field $\mathbb E_N[s_i]=0$. For fixed $r$, subtracting $t^r$ from the formula of step 2.1 gives $(t^{N-r}-t^{N+r})/(1+t^N)$; its absolute value is at most $t^{N-r}+t^{N+r}$ because $0\le t<1$. Thus the fixed-distance limit is $t^r$. When $0<t<1$, writing $t^r=e^{-r/\xi}$ gives $\xi=-1/\log t$; for $J=0$, $t=0$ and all nonzero-separation correlations vanish. [step 2.1, algebra]



3.2 For the field-coupled finite law [A1], differentiating its finite numerator and denominator sums gives $\partial_h\mathbb E_{N,h}[M]=\beta(\mathbb E_{N,h}[M^2]-\mathbb E_{N,h}[M]^2)$, where $M=\sum_i s_i$. At $h=0$, spin-flip symmetry gives $\mathbb E M=0$ and translation invariance gives $$\frac1N\mathbb E[M^2]=1+\sum_{r=1}^{N-1}\mathbb E[s_1s_{1+r}]=1+\frac{2\sum_{r=1}^{N-1}t^r}{1+t^N}.$$ The finite geometric sum tends to $2t/(1-t)$ as $N\to\infty$, so $\chi_N\to\beta(1+t)/(1-t)$. This also gives $\chi_N=\beta$ when $J=0$. [A1, step 2.1, algebra]



4.1 From step 1.1, $N^{-1}\log Z_N=\log(2\cosh(\beta J))+N^{-1}\log(1+t^N)$. Since $1\le1+t^N\le2$, the second term tends to zero; the limit is analytic for every finite $\beta>0$ because $\cosh(\beta J)>0$. The correlation length diverges only in the excluded zero-temperature limit $\beta J\to\infty$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Exact Tonks hard-rod pressure and convergent virial series
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined in [[def-countable-choice]] for the Euclidean Lebesgue product and Jordan-volume identifications below. Use the natural logarithm $\log$ of [[def-natural-logarithm]]. Let $N\ge1$, let $a\ge0$ be a hard-rod length in metres, and let $L>Na$ be the one-dimensional box length in metres. Rod centers are $x_i\in[a/2,L-a/2]$ with $|x_i-x_j|\ge a$ for $i\ne j$. Let each rod have mass $m>0$ kg, momentum $p_i\in\mathbb R$ in kg m s$^{-1}$, and Hamiltonian $H=\sum_{i=1}^Np_i^2/(2m)$ on the allowed configuration set, with infinite energy outside it. Adopt the reference $dx\,dp/(N!h_0^N)$, where $h_0>0$ is a fixed action in J s, and canonical inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$. Put $\lambda=h_0\sqrt{\beta/(2\pi m)}$. Then
$$Z_N=\frac{(L-Na)^N}{N!\lambda^N},\quad U=\mathbb E H=\frac{N}{2\beta},\quad p_{1D}:=-\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial L}\right)_{N,a,m,\beta,h_0}=\frac{N}{\beta(L-Na)},\quad F=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_N.$$
Here $p_{1D}$ is the one-dimensional force conjugate to length and has units N; it is not a three-dimensional pressure. With number density $\rho=N/L$, the exact equation is
$$\beta p_{1D}=\frac{\rho}{1-a\rho}=\sum_{j=1}^\infty a^{j-1}\rho^j,\qquad a\rho<1.$$
After the first $M\ge1$ terms, the exact nonnegative remainder (strictly positive when $a>0$) is $\rho(a\rho)^M/(1-a\rho)$, bounded by $\rho r^M/(1-r)$ whenever $a\rho\le r<1$. At fixed $\rho>0$ with $a\rho<1$, as $N,L\to\infty$ with $N/L=\rho$,
$$\lim\frac{\beta F}{N}=\log\!\left(\frac{\rho\lambda}{1-a\rho}\right)-1,$$
with finite-size excess between $0$ and $(1+\log N)/N$.
items.strategy:
1.1 The single-rod momentum Lebesgue integral is $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-\beta p^2/(2m)}dp=\sqrt{2\pi m/\beta}$ by [F2] and [F8]. By [F5] and Tonelli [F6], the $N$ momentum factors integrate to the product of these integrals. Dividing by $h_0^N$ gives $\lambda^{-N}$. [given, F2, F5, F6, F8, algebra]

1.2 By [F2] and the bounded Riemann-to-Lebesgue agreement in [F8], each normalized scalar momentum Gaussian has second moment $m/\beta$. Thus the mean kinetic energy of each rod is $1/(2\beta)$ and the total mean is $U=N/(2\beta)$. [given, F2, F8, algebra]

1.3 The allowed labelled position set is a finite union of closed bounded ordering polytopes in $[a/2,L-a/2]^N$, hence compact by [F9]. Its boundary is contained in finitely many box faces and contact hyperplanes $x_i-x_j=\pm a$, each a compact graph over a coordinate rectangle, so [F7] makes it Jordan measurable. Fix one label ordering $\pi$ and sort its centers as $x_{\pi(1)}\le\cdots\le x_{\pi(N)}$. On that sector set $y_i=x_{\pi(i)}-a/2-(i-1)a$ and $\ell=L-Na>0$; the hard-core inequalities become the closed bounded, hence compact, ordered simplex $S_\ell:=\{0\le y_1\le\cdots\le y_N\le\ell\}$ by [F9]. Its boundary is contained in the box faces and finitely many tie hyperplanes, each a compact graph over a coordinate rectangle; [F7] therefore makes $S_\ell$ Jordan measurable. The affine permutation map has absolute determinant $1$, so [F3] preserves Jordan volume. The $N!$ coordinate permutations of $S_\ell$ partition $[0,\ell]^N$ up to the tie hyperplanes, which have content zero by [F7]; their equal volumes sum to $\ell^N$, hence each simplex has volume $\ell^N/N!$. The $N!$ labelled order sectors cover the allowed set and overlap only on the stated content-zero contact hyperplanes. Therefore its Jordan content is $\ell^N$, and [F5] gives the full labelled position Lebesgue measure $\ell^N$. [given, A1, F3, F5, F7, F9, algebra]

2.1 The reference measure divides the position-momentum integral by $N!h_0^N$. Product Lebesgue measure and Tonelli [F5, F6] separate the position measure $\ell^N$ from step 1.3 and the momentum integral from step 1.1. Thus $Z_N=\ell^N/(N!\lambda^N)$. [F1, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 By the product, quotient and integer-power laws in [F4], $F=-\beta^{-1}[N\log((L-Na)/\lambda)-\log N!]$, using the logarithm derivative in [F4] at fixed $N,a,\beta$ gives $p_{1D}=N/[\beta(L-Na)]$. Substituting $\rho=N/L$ yields $\beta p_{1D}=\rho/(1-a\rho)$. [F1, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 At $a=0$, the virial series has first term $\rho$ and all higher terms zero, so its remainder after any $M\ge1$ terms is zero. For $0\le a\rho<1$, the finite geometric identity $\sum_{j=1}^M(a\rho)^{j-1}=(1-(a\rho)^M)/(1-a\rho)$ gives the stated virial partial sum and exact remainder after multiplication by $\rho$. If $a\rho\le r<1$, then $(a\rho)^M/(1-a\rho)\le r^M/(1-r)$, proving the uniform bound. [step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 At fixed $\rho>0$, $L-Na=N(1/\rho-a)>0$, so the laws in [F4] give $$\frac{\beta F}{N}=-\log((L-Na)/\lambda)+\frac{\log N!}{N}.$$ For each integer $k=1,\ldots,N-1$, monotonicity of $\log$ bounds its integral on $[k,k+1]$ between $\log k$ and $\log(k+1)$. Summing gives $$\int_1^N\log x\,dx\le\log N!\le\int_1^N\log x\,dx+\log N.$$ For $N=1$ the sums and integral are empty and zero. Since [F4] gives $(x\log x-x)'=\log x$, the integral is $N\log N-N+1$. Hence $\log N!=N\log N-N+\epsilon_N$ with $1\le\epsilon_N\le1+\log N$. Substitution and [F4] cancel $\log N$, yielding $$\frac{\beta F}{N}=\log\!\left(\frac{\rho\lambda}{1-a\rho}\right)-1+\frac{\epsilon_N}{N}.$$ The excess is nonnegative and at most $(1+\log N)/N$. Finally, $\log N=\int_1^Ndx/x\le\int_1^Ndx/\sqrt{x}=2(\sqrt N-1)$, so that upper bound tends to zero and proves the stated thermodynamic limit. [F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Finite spherical-shell gas and its exact marginal
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined in [[def-countable-choice]], the mathematical hypothesis required by the spherical-marginal supplier. Let $N,d\ge1$, $D=dN\ge2$, and let $B=\prod_{j=1}^d[0,L_j]\subset\mathbb R^d$ have side lengths $L_j>0$ in metres and volume $V=\prod_jL_j$ in $\mathrm m^d$. Let $m>0$ kg and $E>0$ joules, and set $R=\sqrt{2mE}$ in kg m s$^{-1}$. Take one operationally indistinguishable species of $N$ particles as specified by [[post-csm-counting-and-physical-observables]]. On the auxiliary labelled cover, take independent uniform positions $q_i\in B$ with density $V^{-1}$ and, independently, the momentum law
$$P=RZ/|Z|,$$
where $Z\in\mathbb R^D$ has the independent standard-normal coordinate law defined in [[thm-csm-examples-spherical-marginal]] and $P=0$ is assigned on the null event $Z=0$. This product law is invariant under particle permutations, so it defines the stated model preparation on the quotient; a one-particle marginal means the law of a uniformly selected particle. This is a specified spherical-shell preparation: $H(P)=|P|^2/(2m)=E$ almost surely, with no assumption about a trajectory or equilibration. For any momentum block of $k$ coordinates with $1\le k<D$, its density is $f_{D,k}$ from [[thm-csm-examples-spherical-marginal]]. In particular the total-energy variance is zero J$^2$.

Compare the separate canonical ideal-gas preparation of [[pthm-csm-ideal-gas-ensemble]] with the same $N,d,m,B$ and one-species convention, at $\beta=D/(2E)>0$. Its mean total energy is also $E$, but its variance is $D/(2\beta^2)>0$ J$^2$. If $N>1$, the uniformly selected particle's $d$-component shell marginal has compact support because $d<D$, whereas its canonical Gaussian momentum has positive probability outside every finite-radius ball. The two finite preparations therefore differ despite their matched mean energy. For $N=1$, the full momentum vector is singular on its sphere and the density formula for $k=D$ is not asserted.
items.strategy:
1.1 Under the shell preparation [F1] and its explicit law [A1], $|P|=R$ almost surely by the definition of $P$; hence $H(P)=R^2/(2m)=E$ on every realization outside the null event $Z=0$. A constant random variable has variance zero. [given, F1, A1, algebra]



2.1 For $1\le k<D$, the first $k$ momentum coordinates are the projection in [F2], so their exact Lebesgue density is the displayed $f_{D,k}$ with support in $|p|\le R$. Its boundary may carry no atom; the underlying Gaussian direction has a density and $Z=0$ is null. [F2, step 1.1]



2.2 Choose $\beta=D/(2E)$. By [F3], the canonical mean energy is $D/(2\beta)=E$ and its variance is $D/(2\beta^2)>0$. Thus it cannot have the shell law of step 1.1, whose energy variance is zero. [given, F3, step 1.1, algebra]



3.1 If $N>1$, then $d<D$ and [F2] gives the one-particle momentum block a density supported in the radius-$R$ ball. By [F3], its canonical Gaussian has strictly positive density at every point of $\mathbb R^d$, so its integral over, for example, the open annulus $R<|p|<2R$ is positive, while the shell probability of that annulus is zero. Therefore the one-particle marginals differ as well. For $N=1$, $d=D$ and the full shell law is singular, so no $k=D$ density assertion has been used. [F2, F3, step 2.1] ∎

David Tong, Statistical Physics, §2.2, canonical ideal-gas momentum distribution

items.title: Unpinned translation zero-mode divergence
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as defined in [[def-countable-choice]] for the Euclidean Lebesgue measure of the phase-space boxes below. Take $N\ge3$ resolved displacement coordinates $q_i\in\mathbb R$ in metres and momenta $p_i\in\mathbb R$ in kg m s$^{-1}$ on a periodic chain, with $q_{N+1}=q_1$, mass $m>0$ kg, spring stiffness $\kappa>0$ in J m$^{-2}$, and
$$H(q,p)=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{p_i^2}{2m}+\frac{\kappa}{2}\sum_{i=1}^N(q_{i+1}-q_i)^2.$$
Adopt inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$ and fixed action reference $h_0=a_0>0$ in J s under [[post-csm-examples-ensemble-preparations]]. Because the coordinates are resolved, use the reference $dq\,dp/h_0^N$ with no particle-exchange factorial. Define the partition integral
$$Z:=\int_{\mathbb R^N\times\mathbb R^N}\exp(-\beta H(q,p))\,\frac{dq\,dp}{h_0^N},$$
where $\exp$ is the real exponential of [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]. The unpinned position integral is infinite, so this model has no normalized canonical probability on the full position space.
items.strategy:
1.1 Put $r_1:=0$ and use coordinates $u:=q_1$, $r_i:=q_i-q_1$ for $2\le i\le N$. The linear bijection $(u,r_2,\ldots,r_N)\mapsto(q_1,\ldots,q_N)=(u,u+r_2,\ldots,u+r_N)$ has determinant $1$. With $r_{N+1}:=r_1$, every periodic difference satisfies $q_{i+1}-q_i=r_{i+1}-r_i$, so the potential is independent of $u$; the momentum term is also independent of $u$. On each compact coordinate box the change-of-variables supplier [F3] therefore gives the phase-volume Jacobian $1$. [given, A1, F3, algebra]



2.1 Under the declared reference convention [F1], choose any compact coordinate box $C$ of positive volume in $(r_2,\ldots,r_N,p)$. The Hamiltonian is continuous and hence bounded above on $C$ by a finite $H_C$ by [F4]. By [F2], $C$ has Lebesgue measure $\operatorname{vol}(C)$. On $u\in[-R,R]$ and $(r,p)\in C$, the integrand is at least $e^{-\beta H_C}$; the determinant-one map in step 1.1 and [F2] show this slab contributes at least $2R e^{-\beta H_C}\operatorname{vol}(C)/h_0^N$ to the partition integral by [F5]. This lower bound is unbounded as $R\to\infty$, so $Z=\infty$ and no normalization exists. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Maxwell speed marginal and Poisson number example
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as required by [[pthm-csm-ideal-gas-ensemble]]. In a canonical sector $N\ge1$ of the massive $d=3$ ideal-gas model of one operationally indistinguishable species, choose any mass $m>0$ in kg and inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$. The most probable speed of a uniformly selected particle is $\sqrt{2/(m\beta)}$ and its ensemble mean speed is $\sqrt{8/(\pi m\beta)}$. In the separate grand model, which includes the vacuum sector, choose the chemical potential
$$\mu_{\rm chem}=\beta^{-1}\log(\lambda^3/V),$$
so the mean activity parameter $\nu=\exp(\beta\mu_{\rm chem})V/\lambda^3$ equals $1$, where $V$ is in m$^3$, $\lambda$ in metres, and $\mu_{\rm chem}$ in joules. The particle count then has the Poisson$(1)$ law, including $\mathbb P(N=0)=\mathbb P(N=1)=\exp(-1)$.
items.strategy:
1.1 Specializing the $d=3$ clauses of [F1] gives the stated mode and mean of the model speed distribution; these are distributional functionals, not values assigned to every individual particle. [F1]

2.1 Substituting [A1] and applying [F2] gives $\exp(\beta\mu_{\rm chem})=\lambda^3/V$, hence $\nu=1$ in [F1]. The Poisson formula then gives $\mathbb P(N=j)=\exp(-1)/j!$, so the $j=0$ and $j=1$ probabilities both equal $\exp(-1)$. [A1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

items.title: Exact finite-ring correlations and limiting correlation length at a chosen coupling
items.design_state: Initial authoring complete; current prerequisite availability and readiness disposition are recorded in batch evidence.
items.statement:
For any finite $N\ge2$ at zero field, choose coupling $J>0$ in joules and inverse temperature $\beta=(\log2)/(2J)$ in J$^{-1}$. Then $t=\tanh(\beta J)=1/3$ and the exact ring correlation at separation $1\le r<N$ is
$$\mathbb E_N[s_i s_{i+r}]=\frac{3^{-r}+3^{-(N-r)}}{1+3^{-N}}.$$
At fixed $r$, the limit is $3^{-r}=e^{-r\log3}$, so the correlation length is $1/\log3$ lattice spacings.
items.strategy:
1.1 Since $\tanh(x)=(e^{2x}-1)/(e^{2x}+1)$, the choice [A1] gives $t=(2-1)/(2+1)=1/3$. [A1, algebra]



2.1 Substituting $t=1/3$ in [F1] gives the displayed finite-$N$ correlation. Its fixed-$r$ limit is $3^{-r}$ by the theorem's error bound, and $3^{-r}=e^{-r\log3}$ gives $\xi=1/\log3$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as required by [[pthm-csm-tonks-rod-ensemble]]. Use the one-species hard-rod model of [[pthm-csm-tonks-rod-ensemble]] with $N\ge1$, rod length $a>0$ in metres, mass $m>0$ in kg, inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$, and fixed action reference $h_0>0$ in J s. Set box length $L=2Na$ in metres. Then $L>Na$ and number density $\rho=N/L=1/(2a)$ in m$^{-1}$, so $a\rho=1/2$. The exact force-conjugate pressure is $\beta p_{1D}=2\rho$. items.strategy:
1.1 The choices give $\rho=N/(2Na)=1/(2a)$ and therefore $a\rho=1/2$. [A1, algebra]

2.1 The exact equation in [F1] gives $\beta p_{1D}=\rho/(1-1/2)=2\rho$. The first two series terms are $\rho+a\rho^2=\rho+\rho/2=3\rho/2$. Applying the remainder formula in [F1] with $M=2$ gives $\rho(1/2)^2/(1-1/2)=\rho/2$, exactly the difference. [F1, step 1.1, A1, algebra] ∎

items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as required by [[pthm-csm-spherical-shell-gas]], and use its one-species rectangular-box model. Take $d=3$, $N=2$, $D=6$, mass $m>0$ in kg, and energy $E>0$ in joules, so the momentum radius is $R=\sqrt{2mE}$ in kg m s$^{-1}$. A uniformly selected particle's three-momentum block ($k=3$) under the shell preparation has density
$$f_{6,3}(p)=\frac{4}{\pi^2R^3}\sqrt{1-\frac{|p|^2}{R^2}},\qquad |p|<R,$$
and zero for $|p|\ge R$. A canonical ideal gas with $\beta=D/(2E)=3/E$ in J$^{-1}$ has the same mean total energy but assigns positive probability to the annulus $R<|p_\star|<2R$ for the uniformly selected particle's momentum $p_\star$.
items.strategy:
1.1 Substituting $D=6,k=3$ into [F1] gives exponent $(6-3-2)/2=1/2$ and coefficient $\Gamma(3)/[\Gamma(3/2)(\pi R^2)^{3/2}]=4/(\pi^2R^3)$ using $\Gamma(3)=2$ and $\Gamma(3/2)=\sqrt\pi/2$. This is the displayed density. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 The shell block has probability zero outside the radius-$R$ ball by [F1]. The canonical Gaussian vector density from [F2] is positive throughout the nonempty annulus $R<|p|<2R$, which has positive volume, so that event has positive canonical probability. Therefore the two finite momentum marginals differ. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎
